long: Pactus has a fixed supply of 42,000,000 PAC, all allocated in the genesis file; there is no minting. Half of it, 21,000,000 PAC, sits in the treasury, which is the all-zero address. Every block reward is paid out of this pre-allocated treasury, and transaction fees are collected back into it before being paid to the proposer. So the total supply never grows: rewards just move coins out of a pot that existed from day one.
tech: Inside #Pactus #1: Pactus has a fixed supply of 42,000,000 PAC, all allocated in the genesis file. Half (21M) sits in the treasury, the all-zero address, and is paid out as block rewards. No minting: rewards come from this pre-allocated pot. #PAC @PactusChain
simple: Inside #Pactus #1: Pactus has a fixed supply: 42M PAC, all created at launch. Nothing new is ever minted. Half sits in a treasury that pays out block rewards over time. #PAC @PactusChain

card.title: Fixed supply, all minted at launch
card.sub: Nothing new is ever created. Half sits in a treasury that pays block rewards.

long: The Pactus block interval is 10 seconds (genesis parameter block_interval_in_second). A block is rejected if the seconds field of its timestamp is not a multiple of that interval. With 10 s, every block time lands on :00, :10, :20, :30, :40 or :50 of a minute, so the slots line up the same way every minute and are easy to reason about.
tech: Inside #Pactus #2: Pactus block time is 10 seconds. A block is rejected unless the seconds field of its timestamp is a multiple of the interval, so blocks always land on the :00, :10, :20… marks of every minute. #PAC @PactusChain
simple: Inside #Pactus #2: A new Pactus block every 10 seconds, on a steady clock: block times always land on the same 10-second marks of each minute. #PAC @PactusChain

card.title: One block, on a steady clock
card.sub: Block times always land on the same 10-second marks of each minute.

long: Block reward (PIP-55), as coded: 1 PAC per block up to height 8,000,000, 0.5 PAC up to 24,000,000, then 0.25 PAC. The schedule depends on block height, not on calendar time. Rewards are paid from the 21M PAC treasury: 8M x 1 + 16M x 0.5 = 16M PAC by block 24M, and the remaining 5M at 0.25 per block lasts 20M more blocks, so at these rates the treasury runs out around block 44M.
tech: Inside #Pactus #3: Pactus block reward (PIP-55), as coded: 1 PAC per block up to height 8M, 0.5 up to 24M, then 0.25. It depends on block height, not calendar time. Rewards come from the 21M PAC treasury, which at these rates runs out around block 44M. #PAC @PactusChain
simple: Inside #Pactus #3: Block rewards shrink over time: 1 PAC per block at first, then 0.5, then 0.25, in steps tied to block count. They come from the 21M PAC treasury, which at these rates lasts until around block 44M. #PAC @PactusChain

card.title: Rewards shrink by block count
card.sub: Paid from the 21M PAC treasury, lasting until around block 44M.

long: The first reward halving is at block 8,000,000. At one block every 10 seconds that is 80M seconds, about 2.5 years after genesis; the second step, at block 24M, is about 7.6 years. Those are lower bounds: when the chain falls behind, the next block takes the current time instead of catching up the missed slots, so the halvings arrive later in real time than this arithmetic says.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #4: The first reward halving is at block 8,000,000: at one block every 10 s that's 80M seconds, about 2.5 years after genesis; the second step, at block 24M, about 7.6 years.

Those are lower bounds. When the chain falls behind, the next block takes the current time instead of catching up missed slots, so halvings arrive later in real time. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #4: The first reward halving comes at block 8 million: about 2.5 years after launch in theory, later in practice.

Blocks missed during slowdowns are not made up: the chain just carries on from the current time. So every delay pushes the halving dates a little further into the future. @PactusChain

card.title: The first halving block
card.sub: About 2.5 years in theory. Later in practice: missed blocks are never made up.

long: Each block's subsidy pays part of the reward to a foundation address. The address is picked as height mod 100 from a list of 100 addresses embedded in the node (one list for mainnet, one for testnet). The base foundation amount is 0.3 PAC per block, and it is multiplied by the same halving coefficient as the block reward, so it drops to 0.15 PAC after block 8M.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #5: Every block's subsidy pays part of the reward to a foundation address, picked as height mod 100 from a list of 100 addresses embedded in the node (one list for mainnet, one for testnet).

The base amount is 0.3 PAC per block, multiplied by the same halving coefficient as the block reward, so it drops to 0.15 PAC after block 8M. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #5: Each block sends a small share of its reward to the foundation, rotating across 100 addresses built into the node.

That share is 0.3 PAC per block at first, and it shrinks along with the block reward: after the first halving at block 8 million, it drops to 0.15 PAC. @PactusChain

card.title: Foundation addresses, in rotation
card.sub: Each block pays a small share to one of them. That share halves with the reward.

long: Every Pactus block must start with exactly one subsidy transaction: a batch transfer signed by no one, sent from the treasury, with a fee of zero. A second subsidy tx in the block is rejected. Validators check it: its total must equal the block reward plus the fees collected in the block, the first recipient must be the right foundation address and amount, and for a delegated validator the stake owner's share must follow the delegation rules.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #6: Every Pactus block must start with exactly one subsidy tx: a batch transfer signed by no one, sent from the treasury, with zero fee. A second one is rejected.

Validators check it: total = block reward + fees in the block, the first recipient must be the right foundation address and amount, and any delegation share must follow the rules. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #6: Every block opens with one special transaction that pays the block reward from the treasury. Nobody signs it and it pays no fee.

Validators check the amounts before accepting the block: the right total, the right foundation share, and the right split if the validator is delegated. Only one per block. @PactusChain

card.title: Every block opens with one subsidy tx
card.sub: Total must equal block reward plus fees.

long: Block timestamps are constrained: the seconds must be a multiple of 10, the time must be strictly after the previous block, and it can be at most one interval later than the expected next slot (previous block time + 10 s). When a proposer finds that more than 10 s have passed since that expected slot, it uses the current time rounded down to the interval. So a block can't pick an arbitrary time, and a stalled chain resumes on the clock.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #7: Block timestamps are constrained: seconds must be a multiple of 10, the time must be strictly after the previous block, and at most one interval past the expected slot (previous time + 10 s).

If more than 10 s have passed since that slot, the proposer uses the current time rounded down. So a stalled chain resumes on the clock. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #7: Block times can't be faked: a block must come after the previous one and close to its expected slot, on a 10-second grid.

If the chain fell behind, the next block simply uses the current time instead of trying to fill the gap. So no proposer can pick an arbitrary time for its block. @PactusChain

card.title: Block time can't be picked freely
card.sub: Seconds a multiple of 10, after the previous block, never far past the next slot.

long: The Pactus mainnet genesis time is 2024-01-24 20:24:00 UTC; testnet started on 2024-03-16 00:00:00 UTC. Both genesis files set the same core parameters: a 10-second block interval and a committee of 51 validators. These values come straight from the genesis JSON files shipped with the node.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #8: Pactus mainnet genesis time is 2024-01-24 20:24:00 UTC; testnet started on 2024-03-16 00:00:00 UTC.

Both genesis files set the same core parameters: a 10-second block interval and a committee of 51 validators. These values come straight from the genesis JSON files shipped with the node. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #8: Pactus mainnet launched on January 24, 2024, and testnet followed on March 16, 2024.

Since then: a block every 10 seconds, secured by a committee of 51 validators at a time. Both networks use these same settings, written into the files the node ships with. @PactusChain

card.title: Validators in the committee
card.sub: Mainnet genesis: 2024-01-24 20:24 UTC, with 10-second blocks.

long: The genesis file has no chain ID field. To know which network it is on, a node hashes the genesis document and compares the hash with the built-in mainnet and testnet genesis hashes; anything else is treated as a localnet. That chain type then sets the address prefix (pc or tpc) and the p2p network name (pactus, pactus-testnet, pactus-localnet). The genesis file is effectively the chain's fingerprint.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #9: The genesis file has no chain ID field. A node hashes the genesis document and compares it with the built-in mainnet and testnet genesis hashes; anything else is a localnet.

That chain type sets the address prefix (pc or tpc) and the p2p network name. The genesis file is effectively the chain's fingerprint. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #9: How does a node know which network it's on? It fingerprints the genesis file, the chain's birth certificate, and compares it with the known mainnet and testnet fingerprints.

Anything else is treated as a local test network. That choice then sets the address prefix and which peers the node talks to. @PactusChain

card.title: No chain ID, the genesis is the ID
card.sub: Nodes hash the genesis file to tell mainnet, testnet and localnet apart.

long: A Pactus block header is always 138 bytes: version (1 byte), time (4), previous block hash (32), state root (32), sortition seed (48, a BLS signature) and proposer address (21). Because the layout is fixed, the store can read a saved block's time at a known offset, right after the block hash and the version byte, without decoding the whole block.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #10: A Pactus block header is always 138 bytes: version (1), time (4), previous block hash (32), state root (32), sortition seed (48, a BLS signature), proposer address (21).

Because the layout is fixed, the store can read a saved block's time at a known offset, right after the block hash and version byte, without decoding the whole block. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #10: Every block starts with a small header of exactly 138 bytes: time, who made it, and fingerprints of the previous block and of the whole chain state.

Because every field always sits at the same place, a node can read a stored block's time directly, without unpacking the whole block. Small and predictable. @PactusChain

card.title: A fixed-size block header
card.sub: Version, time, previous hash, state root, seed, proposer. Always the same layout.

long: A Pactus block hash is the hash of: the encoded header, the hash of the previous block's certificate (absent for the genesis block), the Merkle root of the transactions and the number of transactions. Transactions only enter the block hash through their Merkle root, so changing any transaction changes the root and therefore the block ID.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #11: A Pactus block hash covers the encoded header, the hash of the previous block's certificate (absent for genesis), the Merkle root of the transactions and the tx count.

Transactions only enter the block hash through their Merkle root, so changing any transaction changes the root and therefore the block ID. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #11: A block's ID covers its header, its parent's proof of approval and a fingerprint of all its transactions.

Change a single transaction, even one byte, and that fingerprint changes, so the block ID changes too. Nobody can quietly edit a block's content. @PactusChain

card.title: What a block ID really covers
card.sub: Header, parent's certificate, tx Merkle root and tx count. Change one tx, new ID.

long: Pactus folds a block's transactions into a Merkle root. When a level has an odd number of nodes, the last node is hashed with itself, so a root alone doesn't pin down how many leaves the tree had: duplicating the last item can give the same root. The block hash also includes the transaction count, which closes that known corner case of this kind of Merkle tree.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #12: Pactus folds a block's txs into a Merkle root. When a level has an odd number of nodes, the last one is hashed with itself, so a root alone doesn't pin down the leaf count.

Duplicating the last item can give the same root. The block hash also includes the tx count, which closes that known corner case. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #12: Transactions are folded into one fingerprint, a Merkle root. In this kind of tree, repeating the last item can give the same fingerprint.

So Pactus also adds the number of transactions to the block ID. A block with a duplicated transaction can't pass as the original. @PactusChain

card.title: Why the block hash counts transactions
card.sub: An odd Merkle node is hashed with itself, so the root alone can't fix the leaf count.

long: A Pactus block holds at most 1,000 transactions. The limit appears twice: the block's basic check rejects more than 1,000, and the decoder rejects a transaction-count prefix above 1,000 before it allocates the list. So an oversized block is refused while it is being read, not only later during validation.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #13: A Pactus block holds at most 1,000 transactions. The limit appears twice: the block's basic check rejects more than 1,000.

And the decoder rejects a tx-count prefix above 1,000 before it allocates the list. So an oversized block is refused while it's being read, not only later during validation. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #13: A Pactus block holds at most 1,000 transactions, and nodes reject anything bigger while reading it, before even validating it.

The check happens twice: once when decoding, once when validating. An oversized block can't make a node waste memory before being refused. @PactusChain

card.title: Transactions per block, at most
card.sub: Oversized blocks are refused while being read, before validation even starts.

long: A Pactus block certificate holds the height, the round, the list of committers (committee members, by validator number), the list of absentees and one aggregated BLS signature. There are no per-validator signatures on chain: the signers are the committers minus the absentees, and their signatures are merged into a single one.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #14: A Pactus block certificate holds the height, the round, the committers (committee members, by validator number), the absentees and ONE aggregated BLS signature.

There are no per-validator signatures on chain: the signers are the committers minus the absentees, and their signatures are merged into a single one. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #14: Every block is approved by the committee, but the proof stays tiny: a list of who took part, who was absent, and one combined signature instead of dozens.

The signatures of everyone who approved are merged into one. The chain stays light, even with a full committee. @PactusChain

card.title: One signature for the whole committee
card.sub: A certificate lists committers and absentees, plus one aggregated BLS signature.

long: Verifying a certificate takes one BLS check. The node walks the committee, sums the power of the committers that are not absent, requires at least 2f+1 of the committee power (f = (n-1)/3), aggregates the signers' public keys and verifies the single aggregated signature against them. There is no loop verifying individual signatures, whatever the committee size.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #15: Verifying a Pactus certificate takes one BLS check. The node walks the committee, sums the power of committers not absent, and requires at least 2f+1 of committee power (f = (n-1)/3).

It aggregates the signers' public keys and verifies the single signature against them. No loop over individual signatures, whatever the committee size. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #15: Checking that a block was approved takes a single signature check, however many validators signed.

The node adds up the stake of those who signed, makes sure it's about two thirds of the committee, and verifies one combined signature. That keeps nodes fast and light. @PactusChain

card.title: One BLS check per certificate
card.sub: Sum the signers' power, aggregate their keys, verify once. No loop over signatures.

long: Each Pactus block embeds the certificate that finalised its parent block. When a block is validated, that certificate is checked against the committee of the previous height and must point at the chain's current tip. Only the genesis block has no previous certificate. Block after block, this chains the proofs of approval back to the start.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #16: Each Pactus block embeds the certificate that finalised its parent block. During validation, that certificate is checked against the committee of the previous height and must point at the chain's current tip.

Only the genesis block has no previous certificate. Block after block, this chains the proofs of approval back to the start. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #16: Each block carries the proof that its parent was approved by the committee.

So the chain links itself together, block after block, all the way back to the first one, the only block without such a proof. Every approval is checked when the next block arrives. @PactusChain

card.title: Every block carries its parent's proof
card.sub: The certificate that finalised the parent is embedded. Only genesis has none.

long: Certificates name validators by a compact number (an int32, written as a varint), not by their 21-byte address. Numbers are sequential: genesis validators get the first ones, and a new validator gets the next number when its first bond transaction creates it. Small numbers encode in one or two bytes, which keeps certificates small even with a full 51-member committee.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #17: Certificates name validators by a compact number (int32, written as a varint), not their 21-byte address. Numbers are sequential: genesis validators first, then each new one when its first bond creates it.

Small numbers encode in one or two bytes, which keeps certificates small even with a full 51-member committee. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #17: Validators are referred to by a short number instead of a full address, given in order as each validator is created.

A small number takes one or two bytes, an address takes 21. So block proofs stay small even with a full committee of 51 validators. @PactusChain

card.title: Validators go by number, not address
card.sub: Sequential varint indexes keep certificates small, even with 51 members.

long: Every consensus vote signs block hash + height + round, plus a type tag: PREPARE, PRE-VOTE, MAIN-VOTE or DECIDED (PRECOMMIT has no tag). Change-proposer votes also sign their CP round and value. Because each type signs a different message, a signature made for one vote type can never be replayed as another.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #18: Every consensus vote signs block hash + height + round, plus a type tag: PREPARE, PRE-VOTE, MAIN-VOTE or DECIDED (PRECOMMIT has no tag). Change-proposer votes also sign their CP round and value.

Because each type signs a different message, a signature made for one vote type can never be replayed as another. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #18: Each kind of consensus vote signs a different message: the block, the height, the round and a tag for the vote type.

So a vote cast for one step can never be reused for another. A validator's signature means exactly one thing, at exactly one moment of the vote. @PactusChain

card.title: A vote can't pass for another type
card.sub: Each vote signs block hash, height and round plus its own type tag.

long: Pactus votes are encoded as CBOR maps with fixed integer keys 1 to 7. In transactions, amounts and fees are LEB128 varints, and the decoder rejects non-canonical varints (a zero continuation byte). So each integer has exactly one byte encoding, and every node reads, hashes and signs the very same bytes for the same transaction.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #19: Pactus votes are encoded as CBOR maps with fixed integer keys 1 to 7. In transactions, amounts and fees are LEB128 varints, and the decoder rejects non-canonical varints (a zero continuation byte).

So each integer has exactly one byte encoding, and every node reads, hashes and signs the very same bytes. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #19: Amounts and fees in a transaction have exactly one valid encoding: any other way of writing the same number is rejected.

So every node reads, hashes and signs the very same bytes for the same transaction. One number, one byte form. @PactusChain

card.title: One integer, exactly one encoding
card.sub: Non-minimal varints are rejected, so every node hashes and signs the same bytes.

long: A Pactus transaction ID is the hash of its sign bytes: version, lock time, fee, memo, payload type and payload. The signature and public key are not included. So the ID depends only on what the transaction says, not on how it was signed.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #20: A Pactus transaction ID is the hash of its sign bytes: version, lock time, fee, memo, payload type and payload.

The signature and public key are not included. So the ID depends only on what the transaction says, not on how it was signed. Same content, same ID. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #20: A transaction's ID depends only on what it says: amount, fee, memo and the rest. Not on its signature.

The signature and public key are left out of the fingerprint. So the same transaction always has the same ID, however it was signed, and the ID only changes if the content does. @PactusChain

card.title: Transaction IDs ignore the signature
card.sub: The ID hashes version, lock time, fee, memo and payload. Only what the tx says.

long: Pactus does not vote validators into its committee. After every block, each validator runs a private lottery using its BLS key and the chain's sortition seed. Winners broadcast a sortition transaction to take a seat in the committee. The default committee size, also used on mainnet, is 51 validators.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #21: Pactus doesn't vote validators into its committee. After every block, each validator runs a private lottery using its BLS key and the chain's sortition seed.

Winners broadcast a sortition transaction to take a seat in the committee. The default committee size, also used on mainnet, is 51 validators. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #21: Pactus doesn't elect its validators by vote. After each block, every validator runs a private lottery with its own key and the chain's randomness.

The winners can claim a seat on the committee by sending a special transaction. The committee holds 51 validators on mainnet. @PactusChain

card.title: Committee seats come from a lottery
card.sub: After every block, each validator runs a private draw. Winners claim a seat.

long: The sortition proof is a BLS signature over the seed concatenated with the validator's public key. The proof is hashed with BLAKE2b-256 and scaled into the range [0, total power). With one seed per block, each key gets exactly one deterministic output, and anyone can verify it with the public key, so nobody can rig or repeat their draw.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #22: The sortition proof is a BLS signature over the seed concatenated with the validator's public key, hashed with BLAKE2b-256 and scaled into [0, total power).

With one seed per block, each key gets exactly one deterministic output, and anyone can verify it with the public key, so nobody can rig or repeat their draw. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #22: The committee lottery can't be rigged: each validator's ticket comes from its own key and the chain's randomness, and anyone can check it.

There's exactly one ticket per validator per block. Signing again gives the same result, so trying over and over doesn't help. @PactusChain

card.title: A draw nobody can rig or repeat
card.sub: BLS signature over seed and public key, hashed and scaled. Anyone can verify it.

source: pactus code: sortition/vrf.go (Evaluate, Verify, GetIndex), crypto/hash/hash.go

long: A validator wins sortition when its index, drawn in the range [0, total network power), is below its own power. So the chance to win is power divided by total power: a validator with 10% of the stake wins about 10% of the draws. More stake gives better odds, in direct proportion.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #23: A validator wins sortition when its index, drawn in [0, total network power), is below its own power.

So the chance to win is power divided by total power: a validator with 10% of the stake wins about 10% of the draws. More stake gives better odds, in direct proportion. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #23: More stake means better odds, but fairly: a validator with 10% of the stake wins about 10% of the lottery draws.

Each draw lands somewhere in the total stake of the network, and you win if it falls inside your share. Odds grow in direct proportion to stake. @PactusChain

card.title: Odds match stake, exactly
card.sub: A validator wins when its drawn index is below its own power.

long: Pactus randomness is a chain of BLS signatures. Each block's sortition seed is the proposer's signature over the hash of the previous seed. Before accepting a block, every node verifies that seed against the proposer's public key and the previous seed. Since a BLS signature is deterministic, the proposer can't choose the value.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #24: Pactus randomness is a chain of BLS signatures. Each block's sortition seed is the proposer's signature over the hash of the previous seed.

Before accepting a block, every node verifies that seed against the proposer's public key and the previous seed. Since a BLS signature is deterministic, the proposer can't choose the value. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #24: Where does the randomness come from? Each block's proposer signs the previous random value to make the next one, and every node checks it.

The signature can only come out one way for a given key and input, so the proposer can't pick a value that suits it. No one gets to choose it. @PactusChain

card.title: Randomness built from signatures
card.sub: Each seed is the proposer's BLS signature over the previous seed's hash.

long: A sortition transaction is only valid for a short window: its lock time must be within 17 blocks of the current height, about 3 minutes at 10 s per block. Ordinary transactions get 8,640 blocks, about one day. A lottery win has to be claimed quickly.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #25: A sortition transaction is only valid for a short window: its lock time must be within 17 blocks of the current height, about 3 minutes at 10 s per block.

Ordinary transactions get 8,640 blocks, about one day. A lottery win has to be claimed quickly, or it's gone. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #25: A lottery win must be claimed fast: the ticket expires after 17 blocks, about 3 minutes at one block every 10 seconds.

Normal transactions stay valid for about a day, but a committee seat can't be claimed long after the draw. Win now, claim now, or the seat goes unclaimed. @PactusChain

card.title: A lottery win expires fast
card.sub: About 3 minutes to claim a seat. Ordinary transactions get 8,640 blocks, about a day.

long: A validator must wait 360 blocks after its last bond, about one hour at 10 s per block, before its sortition transactions are accepted. That is the bond_interval genesis parameter, the same on mainnet.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #26: A validator must wait 360 blocks after its last bond, about one hour at 10 s per block, before its sortition transactions are accepted.

That's the bond_interval genesis parameter, the same on mainnet. Fresh stake can't jump straight into the committee lottery. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #26: New validators wait about one hour after staking, 360 blocks, before they can enter the committee lottery.

The rule counts from the latest stake added, so topping up also restarts the wait. Fresh stake can't jump straight into the committee. @PactusChain

card.title: One hour of waiting after a bond
card.sub: Only then are a new validator's sortition transactions accepted.

long: When the committee is full, a sortition tx is only accepted if the power joining in that block stays under one third of committee power, and the power of the members who would leave also stays under one third. The members who leave are those with the oldest sortition height. So at each step less than a third of the committee's power can be replaced, and the longest-seated members rotate out first.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #27: When the committee is full, a sortition tx is only accepted if the power joining in that block stays under one third of committee power, and the power of members who'd leave also stays under one third.

Those who leave have the oldest sortition height. So less than a third can be replaced per step, longest-seated members first. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #27: The committee changes gradually: at each step, less than a third of its power can be replaced.

The members who leave are the longest-seated ones, so newcomers push out the oldest seats, not random ones. The committee never turns over all at once. @PactusChain

card.title: The committee never changes all at once
card.sub: Less than a third of its power can be replaced per step. Oldest seats leave first.

long: While a validator sits in the committee, or is joining it in the current block, bond and unbond transactions for it are rejected in strict checks (block proposal and validation). Its stake is frozen until it leaves the committee: it can't be topped up or unbonded.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #28: While a validator sits in the committee, or is joining it in the current block, bond and unbond txs for it are rejected in strict checks (block proposal and validation).

Its stake is frozen until it leaves the committee: it can't be topped up or unbonded while it helps approve blocks. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #28: While a validator sits on the committee, or is joining it, its stake is frozen: it can't add to it or unstake until it leaves.

So the weight it votes with stays the same for its whole time on the committee. Any change has to wait until it rotates out. @PactusChain

card.title: Stake is frozen while on the committee
card.sub: Bond and unbond transactions for a member are rejected until it leaves.

long: Proposer order is a round-robin walk over a linked list of committee members. Each new member is inserted just before the current proposer position, which puts it at the back of the queue: it gets its first turn after the rest of the committee has had one.

long: The change-proposer timeout grows linearly: 5 s plus 5 s per round (round 0: 5 s, round 1: 10 s, round 2: 15 s), counted from the start of the round. A validator doesn't have to wait for its own timer: if it already sees f+1 change-proposer pre-votes for Yes, it starts changing the proposer right away, so it doesn't join too late.

Values are Yes (change the proposer) or No (keep it); only main-votes can be Abstain. If no decision is reached, it repeats in further change-proposer rounds.

The answer is yes (replace it) or no (keep it). If the committee can't decide, it votes again in another round until it does. @PactusChain

long: Before a round's proposal, validators check the scheduled proposer's availability score. If it is below 0.666667 (PIP-19), they skip the proposal and start changing the proposer for that round straight away. A validator that is often absent effectively loses its turn.

If it's below 0.666667 (PIP-19), they skip the proposal and start changing the proposer for that round straight away. A validator that is often absent effectively loses its turn, and the chain doesn't wait for it. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #43: Validators that are often offline lose their turn: if a proposer's availability score is below two thirds, the committee moves straight to replacing it.

No time is wasted waiting for a block that probably won't come. Showing up regularly is what keeps your turn. @PactusChain

BLS signatures can be aggregated, which is what makes one-signature block certificates possible.

simple:
Inside #Pactus #56: With PIP-50, an account can anchor data on chain: a fingerprint of the data plus a link to it, backed by a deposit of at least 1 PAC.

It goes live once the network upgrades to protocol v5, which needs more than 75% of committee stake running the new version. @PactusChain

card.title: Anchor data on chain with PIP-50
card.sub: A 32 to 64 byte root hash plus a URI up to 128 bytes, backed by a deposit.

long: Pactus has seven transaction types built into the protocol: transfer, bond, unbond, withdraw, sortition, batch transfer and anchor, each with its own executor. Anchor (type 7) is refused as an invalid payload type until blocks reach protocol version 5 (PIP-50).
tech:
Inside #Pactus #57: Pactus has seven transaction types built into the protocol: transfer, bond, unbond, withdraw, sortition, batch transfer and anchor, each with its own executor.

Anchor (type 7) is refused as an invalid payload type until blocks reach protocol version 5 (PIP-50). @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #57: Pactus has 7 built-in transaction types: transfer, stake, unstake, withdraw, committee claim, batch transfer and anchor.

Each one is handled natively by the protocol, each with its own executor and rules. The newest, anchor, waits for protocol v5. @PactusChain

card.title: Transaction types built into the protocol
card.sub: Transfer, bond, unbond, withdraw, sortition, batch transfer and anchor.

long: The default minimum fee is a fixed 0.01 PAC for transfers, bonds, withdrawals, batch transfers and anchors; unbond and sortition pay nothing. The fixed fee is node mempool policy (txpool config), not a consensus rule. The mempool is first-in first-out within each transaction type, so there is no fee auction.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #58: The default minimum fee is a fixed 0.01 PAC for transfers, bonds, withdrawals, batch transfers and anchors; unbond and sortition pay nothing.

The fixed fee is node mempool policy (txpool config), not a consensus rule. The mempool is first-in first-out within each tx type, so there's no fee auction. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #58: Fees are simple: a fixed 0.01 PAC by default, and unstaking is free.

Transactions are taken in arrival order within each type, so paying more doesn't get you in first. No bidding war to get your transaction in, and no guessing the right fee. @PactusChain

card.title: A flat fee, no auction
card.sub: Default minimum for most transactions. Unbond and sortition pay nothing.

long: On top of the fixed fee, the mempool can add a consumption-based fee, driven by how many bytes an account sent over the last 8,640 blocks (about a day). The fee is floor(consumption / 360) x consumption x unit price, so it is zero below the 360-byte daily limit and grows faster than linearly above it. The unit price defaults to 0, so it is off by default.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #59: On top of the fixed fee, the mempool can add a consumption-based fee, driven by how many bytes an account sent over the last 8,640 blocks (about a day).

It's floor(consumption / 360) x consumption x unit price: zero below the 360-byte daily limit, faster than linear above it. Unit price defaults to 0, so it's off. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #59: An optional extra fee can kick in for accounts that send a lot of data in a day, counted over the last 8,640 blocks.

Below about 360 bytes a day it costs nothing; above that, it climbs faster and faster. It's a node setting, and it's off by default. @PactusChain

card.title: An optional fee for heavy senders
card.sub: Zero below the daily limit, faster than linear above it. Off by default.

long: A transaction's lock time is also its expiry: it stays valid for 8,640 blocks after its lock time, about one day at 10 s per block (sortition txs get only 17 blocks). In strict checks a lock time in the future is refused. Memos are capped at 64 bytes.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #60: A transaction's lock time is also its expiry: it stays valid for 8,640 blocks after its lock time, about one day at 10 s per block (sortition txs get only 17 blocks).

In strict checks a lock time in the future is refused. Memos are capped at 64 bytes. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #60: A transaction stays valid for about one day, 8,640 blocks after its lock time. Not included by then? It expires and you can send a new one.

A transaction dated in the future is refused. Memos, the short notes attached to a payment, can be up to 64 bytes. @PactusChain

card.title: Lock time doubles as expiry
card.sub: About one day of validity, only 17 blocks for sortition. Memos up to 64 bytes.

long: A batch transfer pays between 2 and 8 recipients in one signed transaction, and recipient addresses must be distinct. The sender pays the sum of all amounts plus a single fee.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #61: A batch transfer pays between 2 and 8 recipients in one signed transaction, and recipient addresses must be distinct.

The sender pays the sum of all amounts plus a single fee. One signature, one fee, up to eight payments, native to the protocol. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #61: A batch transfer pays 2 to 8 people in one transaction, for a single fee.

Each recipient must be a different address, and the sender pays the total of all amounts plus that one fee. Handy for splitting a payment or paying a small team at once. @PactusChain

card.title: Many recipients, one fee
card.sub: A batch transfer pays distinct addresses in a single signed transaction.

long: The mempool has one bounded sub-pool per transaction type. With the default max_size of 1,000, transfers get 50% (500 slots) and each of the six other types 10% (100 slots), so the pool holds up to 1,100 transactions. When a sub-pool is full, its oldest entry is dropped. A flood of one type can't crowd out the others.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #62: The mempool has one bounded sub-pool per transaction type. With the default max_size of 1,000, transfers get 50% (500 slots) and each of the six other types 10% (100 slots), so the pool holds up to 1,100 txs.

When a sub-pool is full, its oldest entry is dropped. A flood of one type can't crowd out the others. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #62: The waiting room for transactions (the mempool) has a separate lane per type.

Transfers get the biggest lane, and each other type has its own smaller one. When a lane is full, its oldest entry leaves. So a flood of transfers can't crowd out staking or other transactions. @PactusChain

card.title: A separate mempool lane per type
card.sub: Transfers get 500 slots, the six other types 100 each. Full lanes drop the oldest.

long: The proposer takes mempool transactions in a fixed type order: sortition, bond, unbond, withdraw, transfer, batch transfer, anchor, first in first out within each type. It re-checks each one strictly and drops invalid ones, trims the list to 999 and puts the subsidy tx first, for at most 1,000 transactions per block.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #63: The proposer takes mempool txs in a fixed type order: sortition, bond, unbond, withdraw, transfer, batch transfer, anchor; first in first out within each type.

It re-checks each one strictly and drops invalid ones, trims the list to 999 and puts the subsidy tx first, for at most 1,000 transactions per block. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #63: Block proposers pick waiting transactions in a fixed order by type, then first come, first served. No fee auction.

Committee claims and staking come first, then transfers. Each one is checked again, and the block's reward transaction always takes the first spot. @PactusChain

card.title: Proposers pick transactions by type
card.sub: Sortition first, anchor last, first in first out within each. Subsidy tx leads.

long: The state root in each block header combines two Merkle trees, one over accounts and one over validators, hashed with BLAKE2b-256. The trees are persistent and updated incrementally: after a block, only the leaves that changed are set again, so only their paths are rehashed.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #64: The state root in each block header combines two Merkle trees, one over accounts and one over validators, hashed with BLAKE2b-256.

The trees are persistent and updated incrementally: after a block, only the leaves that changed are set again, so only their paths are rehashed. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #64: The whole chain state, all accounts and validators, is summed up in one fingerprint stored in every block.

Updating it only reworks the parts that changed in that block, not the whole thing. So keeping the fingerprint up to date stays cheap as the chain grows. @PactusChain

card.title: Two trees behind the state root
card.sub: Accounts and validators, hashed with BLAKE2b-256. Only changed paths are rehashed.

long: Every account and validator gets a sequential number when it is created (genesis entries first). That number is also its leaf position in the account or validator Merkle tree of the state root.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #65: Every account and validator gets a sequential number when it's created, genesis entries first.

That number is also its leaf position in the account or validator Merkle tree of the state root. One number serves as both ID and leaf position in the state tree. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #65: Every account and validator gets a sequential number when it's created, starting with those at launch.

That number is also its place in the fingerprint of the chain state. One number does two jobs: it identifies the entry and says where it sits. @PactusChain

card.title: Creation order sets the tree position
card.sub: Each account and validator's sequential number is its leaf in the state tree.

long: Pactus writes each committed block in a single LevelDB batch: the block bytes, the tx index, account and validator updates, new public keys and the last-info record with the last certificate. The batch is written atomically, so a crash can't leave these out of sync with each other.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #66: Pactus writes each committed block in a single LevelDB batch: the block bytes, the tx index, account and validator updates, new public keys and the last-info record with the last certificate.

The batch is written atomically, so a crash can't leave these out of sync with each other. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #66: Each block is saved in one atomic write: the block, its transactions' index, balances, validators and the latest proof all go in together.

If a node crashes mid-save, it never ends up half-updated. Either everything is written, or nothing is. @PactusChain

card.title: Each block saved in one atomic write
card.sub: Block, tx index, accounts, validators, keys: one LevelDB batch, crash-safe.

long: The transaction index stores (height, offset, length) for each transaction ID. To read a transaction, the node fetches the stored block bytes for that height and slices out the region directly, without decoding the whole block.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #67: The transaction index stores (height, offset, length) for each transaction ID.

To read a transaction, the node fetches the stored block bytes for that height and slices out the region directly, without decoding the whole block. Only the needed bytes are sliced out, not the whole block decoded. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #67: Looking up a transaction is quick: the node knows exactly where it sits inside its block.

For each transaction it remembers the block height, the position and the length. It just cuts out those bytes instead of unpacking the whole block, however many transactions it holds. @PactusChain

card.title: Reading a transaction without decoding
card.sub: The index stores height, offset and length, so the node slices the block bytes.

long: Each signer's public key is stored once, in a separate index. Once the key is known, the signer's later transactions are saved in the block bytes with the public key stripped, and the key is restored from the index when the block or transaction is read. That saves disk space on every repeat sender.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #68: Each signer's public key is stored once, in a separate index. Once the key is known, the signer's later txs are saved in the block bytes with the public key stripped.

The key is restored from the index when the block or tx is read. That saves disk space on every repeat sender. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #68: Public keys are stored once per account instead of in every transaction, which saves disk space.

The first time an account signs, its key is saved in an index. After that it's left out of stored transactions and added back when they're read. @PactusChain

card.title: Public keys stored once per signer
card.sub: Later transactions drop the key on disk; it's restored from the index on read.

long: In prune mode a node keeps by default the last 30 days of blocks (30 x 8,640 = 259,200 blocks at 10 s), and the retention can't be set below 10 days. The pactus-daemon prune command converts an existing full node to prune mode. Otherwise a node syncing from genesis keeps the full history.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #69: In prune mode a node keeps by default the last 30 days of blocks (30 x 8,640 = 259,200 blocks at 10 s), and retention can't be set below 10 days.

The pactus-daemon prune command converts an existing full node to prune mode. Otherwise a node syncing from genesis keeps the full history. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #69: Short on disk space? A node can be pruned to keep only the last 30 days of blocks, with 10 days as the minimum.

An existing full node can be converted with one command, pactus-daemon prune. Otherwise, nodes keep the full history since launch. @PactusChain

card.title: Prune mode keeps recent blocks only
card.sub: 259,200 blocks by default, never below 10 days. Full history unless you prune.

long: Pactus sync is pull-based: a node that falls behind asks peers for blocks over direct streams, in download sessions, instead of having blocks pushed to it. Gossip is only used for fresh data: new-block announcements, transactions and consensus messages.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #70: Pactus sync is pull-based: a node that falls behind asks peers for blocks over direct streams, in download sessions, instead of having blocks pushed to it.

Gossip is only used for fresh data: new-block announcements, transactions and consensus messages. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #70: Catching up is pull-based: a node that falls behind asks peers for the blocks it misses, over direct connections.

Gossip, the broadcast channel, is only for fresh news: new blocks, transactions and votes. Old history isn't flooded across the whole network. @PactusChain

card.title: Sync pulls, gossip pushes
card.sub: A lagging node asks peers for blocks. Gossip carries only new blocks, txs and votes.

long: Pactus gossip uses three libp2p gossipsub topics: block, transaction and consensus. Topic names include the network name (pactus, pactus-testnet or pactus-localnet), so mainnet, testnet and local networks never share a gossip channel.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #71: Pactus gossip uses three libp2p gossipsub topics: block, transaction and consensus.

Topic names include the network name (pactus, pactus-testnet or pactus-localnet), so mainnet, testnet and local networks never share a gossip channel, even when their nodes connect. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #71: Pactus nodes gossip on three channels: blocks, transactions and consensus.

Each network has its own channel names, built from the network's name. So mainnet, testnet and local test networks never mix their messages, even if their nodes meet. @PactusChain

card.title: Gossip topics, one set per network
card.sub: Block, transaction and consensus topics carry the network name, so they never mix.

long: Every Pactus P2P message travels in the same CBOR envelope (a bundle) with four fields: flags, message type, payload and consensus height. Each message type declares whether it is gossiped on a topic or sent point to point to one peer.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #72: Every Pactus P2P message travels in the same CBOR envelope (a bundle) with four fields: flags, message type, payload and consensus height.

Each message type declares whether it's gossiped on a topic or sent point to point to one peer. One envelope for every message on the network. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #72: All Pactus network messages share one envelope format: a few flags, the message type, the content and the current height.

Each message type also knows whether it's broadcast to everyone or sent to a single peer. One format for every message. @PactusChain

card.title: One envelope for every message
card.sub: Flags, type, payload and height. Each type knows if it's gossiped or sent to one peer.

long: A node catching up opens up to 8 parallel download sessions, each asking for 720 blocks, and the serving peer answers in messages of 60 blocks. It never opens two sessions with the same peer, so downloads are spread across peers.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #73: A node catching up opens up to 8 parallel download sessions, each asking for 720 blocks, and the serving peer answers in messages of 60 blocks.

It never has two open sessions with the same peer at once, so concurrent downloads come from different peers. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #73: A node catching up downloads from several peers at once: up to 8 parallel batches of 720 blocks, sent back 60 at a time.

It never asks the same peer for two batches at the same time, so the load is spread across peers. @PactusChain

card.title: Catching up in parallel
card.sub: Up to 8 download sessions at once, served in 60-block messages.

long: Blocks are downloaded in parallel but committed in strict order. Received blocks and certificates wait in LRU caches keyed by height, and the node commits the next height only when both the block and its certificate are in the cache, then moves on to the following one.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #74: Blocks are downloaded in parallel but committed in strict order. Received blocks and certificates wait in LRU caches keyed by height.

The node commits the next height only when both the block and its certificate are in the cache, then moves on to the following one. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #74: Blocks may arrive out of order, but they are always added to the chain in order, each with its proof.

Blocks that arrive early wait in a cache until the ones before them are in, and a block is only added once its proof of approval is there too. Fast download, strict order. @PactusChain

card.title: Downloaded in parallel, committed in order
card.sub: Each height is committed only once its block and certificate are both cached.

long: Download peers are picked at random, weighted by their download score: (completed sessions + 1) x 100 / (total sessions + 1), an integer percent. A new peer starts at 100. A peer that keeps failing sinks toward 0 and is picked less and less. A request is only sent to a peer that completed the handshake.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #75: Download peers are picked at random, weighted by their download score: (completed sessions + 1) x 100 / (total sessions + 1), an integer percent.

A new peer starts at 100. A peer that keeps failing sinks toward 0 and is picked less and less. Requests only go to peers that completed the handshake. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #75: For downloads, nodes favour peers that delivered reliably.

Each peer gets a score from its track record. Newcomers start with full credit; peers that keep failing get picked less and less, but the choice stays random, so no single peer gets all the work. @PactusChain

card.title: Reliable peers get picked more
card.sub: Download score starts at 100 and sinks toward 0 for a peer that keeps failing.

long: Nodes advertise a FULL flag when they keep the whole chain history (not pruned). A node more than 86,400 blocks behind, about 10 days at 10 s, downloads only from FULL peers, because pruned nodes may not have those blocks. Within that window, any handshaken peer, pruned or full, can serve it.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #76: Nodes advertise a FULL flag when they keep the whole chain history (not pruned).

A node more than 86,400 blocks behind, about 10 days at 10 s, downloads only from FULL peers, because pruned nodes may not have those blocks. Within that window, any handshaken peer, pruned or full, can serve it. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #76: Very far behind, about 10 days or more? A node then downloads only from peers that keep the full history, which they announce with a flag.

Pruned nodes may have deleted those old blocks. For a smaller gap, any connected peer can help, pruned or not. @PactusChain

card.title: Far behind, only full nodes will do
card.sub: About 10 days back, pruned peers may lack the blocks, so FULL peers serve them.

long: Handshake: the outbound peer sends Hello; the inbound peer replies with a HelloAck and sends its own Hello; the outbound peer acks it. A peer only becomes known once the Hellos are accepted, and only known peers are used to request or serve blocks.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #77: Handshake: the outbound peer sends Hello; the inbound peer replies with a HelloAck and sends its own Hello; the outbound peer acks it.

A peer only becomes known once the Hellos are accepted, and only known peers are used to request or serve blocks. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #77: Before exchanging blocks, two nodes say hello and acknowledge each other, in both directions: hello, ack, hello, ack.

Only peers that complete this handshake are used for syncing. A node that skips it can't ask for blocks or be asked for them. @PactusChain

card.title: A handshake before any block
card.sub: Hello, HelloAck, Hello, ack. Only known peers request or serve blocks.

long: For NAT, a Pactus node by default enables libp2p AutoNAT v2 to detect whether it is reachable, and relay support is on by default, with auto-relay and hole punching, so a node behind a home router can still be reached. UPnP port mapping exists but is opt-in (off by default).
tech:
Inside #Pactus #78: For NAT, a Pactus node enables libp2p AutoNAT v2 by default to detect whether it's reachable.

Relay support is on by default, with auto-relay and hole punching, so a node behind a home router can still be reached. UPnP port mapping exists but is opt-in (off by default). @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #78: Behind a home router? Pactus nodes detect it and use relays and hole punching to stay reachable.

That's on by default, so a node behind a home router can still be reached. Automatic port opening (UPnP) also exists, but you have to turn it on. @PactusChain

card.title: Reachable even behind a home router
card.sub: AutoNAT v2 detects it, then relays and hole punching. UPnP is opt-in.

long: Connection limits by default: up to 64 inbound connections (max_connections), and outbound dials up to a quarter of that, 16. Every 60 seconds the node checks connectivity; if fewer than 14 peers (64/4 - 2) are connected, it redials its saved and bootstrap peers in the background.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #79: Connection limits by default: up to 64 inbound connections (max_connections), and outbound dials up to a quarter of that, 16.

Every 60 seconds the node checks connectivity; if fewer than 14 peers (64/4 - 2) are connected, it redials its saved and bootstrap peers in the background. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #79: Nodes cap their connections: 64 incoming by default, and 16 outgoing, a quarter of that.

Every minute they check how many peers they have. If they drop below 14, they automatically reconnect to peers they know and to bootstrap peers, in the background. @PactusChain

card.title: Connection caps, with auto-redial
card.sub: Inbound by default, outbound up to 16. Below 14 peers, the node redials.

long: A node keeps a peer store in peers.json: on clean shutdown it saves the peers it connected to, plus the bootstrap entries, and at startup it loads them along with the bootstrap list. The mainnet bootstrap list (bootstrap.json) is embedded in the binary with go:embed.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #80: A node keeps a peer store in peers.json: on clean shutdown it saves the peers it connected to, plus the bootstrap entries.

At startup it loads them along with the bootstrap list. The mainnet bootstrap list (bootstrap.json) is embedded in the binary with go:embed. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #80: A node remembers its peers when it shuts down cleanly, saving them to a file, and reconnects to them at the next start.

For a first start, the mainnet list of entry peers is built into the program itself. No setup needed to find the network. @PactusChain

card.title: Nodes remember their peers
card.sub: Saved to peers.json on clean shutdown. Mainnet's bootstrap list is in the binary.

long: The node API is defined once, in .proto files. A single buf generate run produces the gRPC stubs, the REST gateway, JSON-RPC bindings, OpenAPI and OpenRPC specs and the docs. So all the API surfaces come from one definition and stay in sync.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #81: The node API is defined once, in .proto files. A single buf generate run produces the gRPC stubs, the REST gateway, JSON-RPC bindings, OpenAPI and OpenRPC specs and the docs.

So all the API surfaces come from one definition and stay in sync. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #81: The node's API is defined once, and gRPC, REST, JSON-RPC and the docs are all generated from that single definition.

Change the definition, run one command, and every interface and its documentation update together. One source, always in sync. @PactusChain

card.title: One API definition, every interface
card.sub: From .proto files, one buf generate builds gRPC, REST, JSON-RPC and the docs.

long: The node's gRPC API has 5 services (blockchain, network, transaction, wallet, utils) and 54 RPCs. The wallet service is opt-in (enable_wallet = false). With mainnet defaults only gRPC is enabled, bound to 127.0.0.1:50051 (local machine only); REST, JSON-RPC and ZeroMQ are off. Testnet defaults differ.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #82: The node's gRPC API has 5 services (blockchain, network, transaction, wallet, utils) and 54 RPCs. The wallet service is opt-in (enable_wallet = false).

With mainnet defaults only gRPC is enabled, bound to 127.0.0.1:50051 (local machine only); REST, JSON-RPC and ZeroMQ are off. Testnet defaults differ. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #82: Out of the box, a mainnet node only opens its main API, gRPC, to the local machine, on 127.0.0.1.

The wallet service, REST, JSON-RPC and live feeds are all off until you turn them on in the config. No API is exposed to the internet by default. @PactusChain

card.title: Local-only API by default
card.sub: Mainnet nodes open only gRPC, on 127.0.0.1:50051. The wallet service is opt-in.

long: Pactus also exposes JSON-RPC and REST. The JSON-RPC server is a thin layer over the node's own gRPC server, and the REST gateway ships with a Swagger UI embedded in the binary via go:embed, giving developers an interactive API page served by the node itself.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #83: Pactus also exposes JSON-RPC and REST. The JSON-RPC server is a thin layer over the node's own gRPC server.

The REST gateway ships with a Swagger UI embedded in the binary via go:embed, giving developers an interactive API page served by the node itself. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #83: Developers also get JSON-RPC and REST, on top of the main gRPC API, which JSON-RPC simply wraps.

The REST side comes with an interactive Swagger page built into the node itself, so you can try API calls from your browser without installing anything else. @PactusChain

card.title: JSON-RPC and REST, Swagger included
card.sub: JSON-RPC wraps the node's gRPC server; the Swagger UI is embedded in the binary.

long: Nodes can publish committed blocks and their transactions over ZeroMQ, on 5 feeds: block info, transaction info, raw block, raw transaction and anchor info, each tagged with a 2-byte topic ID. It is off by default. The implementation uses the pure-Go zmq4 library, with no libzmq dependency. The raw-block feed carries the header only.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #84: Nodes can publish committed blocks and their txs over ZeroMQ, on 5 feeds: block info, tx info, raw block, raw tx and anchor info, each tagged with a 2-byte topic ID.

Off by default. It uses the pure-Go zmq4 library, with no libzmq dependency. The raw-block feed carries the header only. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #84: Apps can subscribe to a live feed of new blocks and transactions over ZeroMQ, instead of asking the node again and again.

There are 5 feeds, including raw data and one for anchors. It's off by default and needs no extra library on the machine. @PactusChain

card.title: Live block feeds over ZeroMQ
card.sub: Block, tx, raw block, raw tx and anchor info. Off by default, pure Go.

long: pactus-shell is a command-line gRPC client with an interactive prompt mode. Its commands are generated from the same .proto services as the gRPC API, so once the code is regenerated and rebuilt, the shell follows the API.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #85: pactus-shell is a command-line gRPC client with an interactive prompt mode.

Its commands are generated from the same .proto services as the gRPC API, so once the code is regenerated and rebuilt, the shell follows the API. No hand-written command list to fall out of date. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #85: pactus-shell lets you query a node from the command line, with an interactive mode.

Its commands are generated from the same definition as the node's API, so every API call is available in the shell too, and stays that way after updates. @PactusChain

card.title: Query a node from the command line
card.sub: pactus-shell commands are generated from the same .proto services as the API.

long: The wallet reaches the chain through a provider. There are three: a local node, a remote provider using a list of gRPC servers, and an offline provider that makes no network calls at all.
tech:
Inside #Pactus #86: The wallet reaches the chain through a provider. There are three: a local node, a remote provider using a list of gRPC servers.

And an offline provider that makes no network calls at all. The same wallet code works whether you run your own node, rely on public servers, or stay fully offline. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #86: The wallet can talk to your own node, to a list of public servers, or work fully offline.

In offline mode it makes no network calls at all. You choose how much you rely on others, from running everything yourself to never touching the network. @PactusChain

card.title: Three ways for a wallet to reach the chain
card.sub: Through a local node, a list of remote gRPC servers, or fully offline.

long: Before starting (and also before pruning or importing), pactus-daemon takes an exclusive file lock on .pactus.lock in its working directory. If a second instance tries to use the same data, the lock fails: it prints a warning that another instance may be running and exits.

long: The Pactus Docker image is a two-stage build: a golang Alpine builder compiles pactus-daemon, pactus-wallet and pactus-shell as static binaries (CGO disabled, -trimpath, stripped with -s -w), then copies them into a plain alpine image.

Then they're copied into a plain alpine image, with no build tools left inside. @PactusChain
simple:
Inside #Pactus #88: The official Docker image is small: the node, wallet and shell are built as standalone programs, then copied onto plain Alpine Linux.

The tools used to build them are left behind in a first stage, so the final image only holds what's needed to run. @PactusChain
